newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan frees Islamist leaders as sit-in fails.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan frees Islamist leaders as sit-in fails.

text.p: The Pakistani government released three leaders of a fundamentalist Islamist party on Monday as their plans to stage a million-strong protest sit-in in Islamabad fizzled out.
But the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) party said it would still launch a nationwide movement against Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's government.

The police arrested Jamaat-i-Islami leader Qazi Hussain Ahmed and his deputies Khurshid Ahmed and Ghafoor Ahmed on a second day of chaotic skirmishes with militants in Islamabad and nearby Rawalpindi in which at least 50 people were injured.
Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar told reporters the three men were freed after about two hours detention at a rest house outside Islamabad.
The Jamaat-i-Islami had vowed to bring a million people to Islamabad to protest against alleged government corruption.

But after two days of struggle against a heavy deployment of security forces, only a few hundred activists could reach the venue before dusk on Monday and they were dispersed by volleys of police tear gas.
About 35 people were injured in police baton and tear gas charges in Rawalpindi and about 15 in Islamabad, staff of the private Edhi ambulance service said.

Baber, quoted by the official APP news agency, said security measures would remain in force unless the sit-in programme was abandoned completely. "It is our inherent responsibility to provide protection to the life and property of people," he said.
Hussain Ahmed told reporters after his release that he would address a rally in Rawalpindi on Tuesday and would announce his party's next actions.

A Jamaat-i-Islami spokesman told Reuters earlier the party would launch an anti-government campaign across Pakistan from Tuesday. Protesting women and children would gather in front of parliament on November 11 and recite the Koran, he added.
Throughout the day security forces blocked access roads to the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching parliament.
Jamaat-i-Islami militants fought cat-and-mouse battles with police in the Aabpara district of the capital. They burned tyres and wooden crates as police on rooftops fired tear gas at them.
Police hunting for young militants searched a mosque and detained several people in the streets, apparently at random.
Demonstrators caught one policeman and beat him, finally letting him run off with his trousers in tatters. They seized a tear gas launcher from another policeman, but could find no ammunition for it.
Several tear gas canisters fell among houses in the residential district, where one woman carrying a child rushed in panic out of her house, tears streaming from her eyes.
At least 29 people were injured in similar clashes on Sunday and newspapers said up to 100 had been hurt, none seriously.
Paramilitary troops were brought into the capital to guard parliament, the prime minister's secretariat, the president's house, the foreign ministry and the diplomatic enclave.
Most schools and universities in Islamabad remained closed for a second day and many people did not go to work.
